You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE conductor (
    Conductor_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Age INT,
    Nationality TEXT,
    Year_of_Work INT,
    UNIQUE (Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE orchestra (
    Orchestra_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra TEXT,
    Conductor_ID INT,
    Record_Company TEXT,
    Year_of_Founded REAL,
    Major_Record_Format TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Orchestra_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Conductor_ID) REFERENCES conductor(Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE performance (
    Performance_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra_ID INT,
    Type TEXT,
    Date TEXT,
    Official_ratings_(millions) REAL,
    Weekly_rank TEXT,
    Share TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Performance_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Orchestra_ID) REFERENCES orchestra(Orchestra_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE show (
    Show_ID INT,
    Performance_ID INT,
    If_first_show bool,
    Result TEXT,
    Attendance REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (Performance_ID) REFERENCES performance(Performance_ID)
);

There isn’t a `famous` flag in the schema, so I can’t directly filter “famous conductors” unless we define what “famous” means (e.g., highest TV ratings, most performances, most attendance, best results).

Meanwhile, here are a few useful SQL options:

### 1) List all conductors (basic)
```sql
SELECT Conductor_ID, Name, Age, Nationality, Year_of_Work
FROM conductor
ORDER BY Name;
```

### 2) “Famous” by most performances (conductors whose orchestras performed most)
```sql
SELECT c.Conductor_ID, c.Name, COUNT(p.Performance_ID) AS performance_count
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY performance_count DESC;
```

### 3) “Famous” by highest average official ratings
```sql
SELECT c.Conductor_ID, c.Name,
       AVG(p."Official_ratings_(millions)") AS avg_official_ratings_millions
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY avg_official_ratings_millions DESC;
```

### 4) “Famous” by total attendance (from shows)
```sql
SELECT c.Conductor_ID, c.Name,
       SUM(s.Attendance) AS total_attendance
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
JOIN show s ON s.Performance_ID = p.Performance_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY total_attendance DESC;
```

Which definition of “famous” do you want (most performances, highest ratings, highest attendance, etc.), and do you want the top N (e.g., top 10)?
just need the names of conductors that fit the idea of famous

Since the schema doesn’t store “famous” directly, a reasonable proxy is: conductors whose orchestras have the highest overall official ratings. This returns just their names:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY AVG(p."Official_ratings_(millions)") DESC;
```

If you want “famous” to mean something else (most performances, highest attendance, top weekly rank), tell me which and I’ll adjust.
We should only look at conductors who have worked with multiple orchestras, not just one.

```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1
ORDER BY c.Name;
```
Just to clarify, we need to focus only on conductors who have been involved with multiple orchestras.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) >= 2
ORDER BY c.Name;
```
